body.en:
Why Successive Multipliers & Harmonic Average Speed Work: If a quantity \(Q_0\) undergoes a percentage change \(p\%\) followed by \(q\%\), the compound multiplier is the product of individual scale factors:

\[ Q_{\text{final}} = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\!\left(1 + \frac{q}{100}\right) = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p + q}{100} + \frac{pq}{10000}\right) \]

Notice the cross term \(\dfrac{pq}{10000}\): an increase of \(p\%\) followed by a decrease of \(p\%\) yields \(Q_0\bigl(1 - (p/100)^2\bigr) < Q_0\). Similarly, traveling equal distance \(d\) at speeds \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) takes total time \(T = \frac{d}{v_1} + \frac{d}{v_2}\), so average speed is the harmonic mean \(v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{2d}{d/v_1 + d/v_2} = \dfrac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

Write \( 0.000452 \) in standard form.

Move the decimal point four places right to land between 4 and 5, so the exponent is \( -4 \):

\[ 0.000452 = 4.52\times 10^{-4}. \]

A coat costs $60 after a 20% discount. Find its original price.

The sale price is 80% of the original, so divide rather than add back 20%:

\[ \text{original}=\frac{60}{0.8}=\$75. \]

A surd is an irrational root left in exact form (e.g. \(\sqrt{3}\)). Key rules: \(\sqrt{ab}=\sqrt{a}\cdot\sqrt{b}\); \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{a}}{a}\) (rationalising a denominator). To rationalise \(\dfrac{p}{a+\sqrt{b}}\), multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(a-\sqrt{b}\).

A length is measured as \(12.4\) cm, rounded to 1 d.p. State the upper and lower bounds.

Half the smallest unit = 0.05.
Lower bound: \(12.35\) cm.   Upper bound: \(12.45\) cm.

Dividing by a negative number reverses order on the real number line.
Flip the inequality symbol whenever multiplying or dividing by a negative: \(x < -4\).
Computing round-trip average speed as \(\frac{v_1 + v_2}{2}\)
Time spent at the slower speed is longer than time spent at the faster speed.
Use total distance over total time: \(v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

body.en: High-Speed Exam Shortcut (Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580 Extended)): When a linear system asks for a combined expression like \(3x + 3y\) rather than \(x\) and \(y\) individually, add or subtract the two equations directly before isolating either variable—this often yields the target expression in a single step.

body.en:
Significant Figures vs. Decimal Places: Unless specified otherwise, Cambridge IGCSE demands answers to 3 significant figures (or 1 d.p. for angles). Leading zeros are NOT significant: \(0.00350\) has 3 s.f., while \(350\) is ambiguous unless written in standard form \(3.50 \times 10^2\).

Limits of Accuracy: For division \(\frac{A}{B}\), the maximum possible value occurs when the numerator is at its upper bound and the denominator is at its lower bound: \(\text{Max} = \frac{A_{\text{upper}}}{B_{\text{lower}}}\). Never round intermediate values during multi-step bound calculations.

question.en: A car travels a distance of \(d = 180\text{ km}\) correct to the nearest 10 km in a time of \(t = 2.4\text{ hours}\) correct to 1 decimal place. Calculate the upper bound for the average speed of the car in km/h.

solution.en:
Find the bounds for distance and time:

\[d_{\text{upper}} = 180 + 5 = 185\text{ km}\]\[t_{\text{lower}} = 2.4 - 0.05 = 2.35\text{ hours}\]

To maximize speed \(s = \frac{d}{t}\), divide the upper distance by the lower time:

\[s_{\text{upper}} = \frac{185}{2.35} \approx 78.723\dots \approx 78.7\text{ km/h (3 s.f.)}\]

hints.en: Find the bounds for distance and time: \(d_{\text{upper}} = 180 + 5\).
To maximize speed \(s = \frac{d}{t}\), divide the upper distance by the lower time: \(s_{\text{upper}} = \frac{185}{2.35}\).

The arrow points directly to the mark labelled '0'.
